source.title: Latent State Models of Training Dynamics
source.authors: Michael Y Hu; Angelica Chen; Naomi Saphra; Kyunghyun Cho

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: The study's own experiments refine when a memorization/generalization gap appears: in its grokking tasks, adding layer normalization and decreasing batch size reduce the gap, while these interventions also change convergence dynamics. It does not test random-label memorization or the other catalog versions directly.
record.gate_note: The paper reports that grokking models first memorize training data and later generalize, and directly compares stabilized and unstabilized grokking/image-classification training. It reports no random-label experiments. Results cited from prior work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study measures training trajectories, seed sensitivity, grokking delays, and convergence times. None tests V1–V8. In particular, grokking is not the random-label comparison in V1; the joint batch-size and normalization intervention does not measure V5's held-out performance under fixed epoch budgets; and sharpness is conjectured rather than measured as required by V7.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially accurate. The authors propose HMM representations of training dynamics and identify optional detour states associated with slower convergence and seed sensitivity. Architecture and hyperparameter changes can remove or induce these states, and the joint modular-addition intervention substantially reduces grokking delay. Their explanation involving a sharp optimization landscape is a conjecture, not a measured sharpness result.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies HMM representations of training trajectories, convergence timing, and grokking; it does not test the claim's interventions or measures on random-label memorization and natural-label test generalization.
record.method_sensitivity: Training trajectory and convergence vary with random seed and with architectural or hyperparameter changes: adding layer normalization and reducing batch size for modular addition, and removing batch normalization and residual connections for CIFAR-100.

fits_no_version.finding: Initial latent-state transitions distinguish faster and slower generalization in modular addition and sparse parities, with different early L2-norm changes.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In these algorithmic tasks, early weight-norm dynamics and inferred state paths correlate with the timing of generalization.

fits_no_version.finding: Adding layer normalization and reducing batch size jointly accelerates modular-addition convergence by approximately 30-fold and removes inferred path forks; removing normalization and residual connections induces variability in CIFAR-100 training.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Architecture and optimization choices can change grokking delays and sensitivity of convergence dynamics to random seed.

fits_no_version.finding: Latent-state occupancy predicts convergence time strongly in forked settings, moderately in stabilized modular addition, and poorly in standard CIFAR-100.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Associations between latent-state occupancy and convergence time depend on the training setup; optional states with positive regression coefficients identify detours.

fits_no_version.finding: MNIST runs share an inferred state path, while MultiBERTs exhibit internal trajectory differences despite similar pretraining-loss evolution.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Latent training-state analysis can characterize seed variation that differs across tasks and may be invisible in training loss.

record.problems: No experiments use random labels or directly quantify train-test error gaps on natural labels. For some results, exact values are summarized in figures/tables while uncertainty and detailed accuracy trajectories are not given in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No reported claim-relevant results were left out. Some paper results, such as state-transition feature changes not directly reporting the convergence or memorization/generalization outcome, were omitted.

untested.parts: Matched random-label and natural-label training, random-label fit, and their held-out accuracy comparison.
Width sweeps beyond zero training error and resulting test-error changes.
Convolutional versus fully connected image-classification performance and the role of local connectivity or initialization.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer comparisons under specified tuning budgets and recovery interventions.
Batch-size effects on held-out performance under fixed epoch budgets and whether adapted recipes remove a penalty.
Dropout effects on held-out error across dataset sizes, dropout strengths, and augmentation conditions.
Magnitude-aware weight-perturbation sharpness, its association with generalization gaps, and comparisons with norm- and margin-based measures.
Retraining after removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: All row states are assessed relative to V1–V8: cannot_determine indicates that the measures cannot establish those effects, even where the reported trajectory finding is clear. No version-level verdict is warranted.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and test performance on natural labels.
Convolutional versus fully connected architecture comparison.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD generalization comparison.
Large versus small batch held-out performance under fixed epoch budgets.
Dropout intervention and its held-out error effects.
Magnitude-aware sharpness comparisons against generalization gaps.
Removing memorized examples and comparing test accuracy.

rows.subject: one-layer autoregressive transformer
rows.size_stated: one layer; hidden size 128; 4 heads; head size 32
rows.operation_detail: Trained on modular addition; compared paths associated with differing convergence epochs.
rows.note: Authors relate path differences to the timing of generalization; this is a grokking-task result rather than held-out error gap across natural labels.
rows.check: The numbers match Figure 2, but the listed edges group trajectories by their initial transition, rather than specifying complete paths. Convergence timing does not measure any claim version.

rows.subject: one-layer autoregressive transformer
rows.size_stated: one layer; hidden size 128; 4 heads; head size 32
rows.operation_detail: Added layer normalization and reduced batch size; compared convergence dynamics on modular addition.
rows.baseline: Original setup: batch size 2048, no layer normalization
rows.value: Converges around 30 times faster; sensitivity to random seed disappears and training map becomes linear
rows.note: The text also says the map continues to reflect memorization and generalization phase transitions.
rows.check: Section 3.3 and Table 6 support the joint normalization and batch-size intervention and approximately 30-fold speedup. Figure 5's caption instead mentions a lower learning rate, an internal inconsistency. The intervention does not isolate batch size or compare held-out performance at a fixed epoch budget.

rows.subject: ResNet18
rows.operation_detail: Removed batch normalization and residual connections; compared convergence paths on CIFAR-100.
rows.note: Removing both components made training more sensitive to randomness; the paths had different convergence times.
rows.check: Values match Figure 4. These are convergence-step summaries grouped by transitions, not complete mutually exclusive paths; some runs visit both transitions. They do not measure any claim version.

rows.subject: ResNet18

rows.value: All 40 training runs follow the same path
rows.note: The paper says individual runs can spend slightly different amounts of time in each state.
rows.check: The shared inferred state path is correctly reported, but it measures training dynamics rather than any version's generalization effect.

rows.subject: sparse-parities MLP

conditions.value: AND of 3 relevant bits in a 40-length bit vector

rows.measure: Path and feature changes associated with generalization timing
rows.value: Slow runs take 2→0→5; fast runs take 2→5; the 2→0 edge increases L2 norm and 2→5 decreases it
rows.note: The result concerns a synthetic algorithmic task and the timing of its generalization phase transition.
rows.check: The paths and norm-change directions match the text. Generalization timing and unscaled weight norms do not measure V1's random-label comparison or V7's magnitude-aware sharpness.
